# Datasets: structure, variable types, file formats {#sec-ch-ml-data}

> *"Tidy datasets are all alike, but every messy dataset is messy in its own
> way."* — Hadley Wickham [@wickham2014].

```{python}
#| echo: false
import mlbook
mlbook.setup()
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

- tell **structured**, **semi-structured** and **unstructured** data apart,
  and explain how images, text and sound are turned into tables of numbers;
- organise data as a **tidy** table — one row per observation, one column per
  variable — and reshape a messy table with pandas;
- classify every variable by **type** (nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio;
  discrete or continuous) and **prove** which summaries are meaningful for
  each type;
- describe a variable by location, spread and **skewness**, and prove how
  skewness behaves under changes of unit;
- read **CSV/TSV, JSON, XML, HTML and Excel** files into a `DataFrame`,
  handling separators, decimal marks, encodings, nesting and missing markers;
- take a disciplined **first look** at a new data set.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Topics covered
The kinds of data a machine-learning project meets — structured and
unstructured — and the types of variables they contain; in practice, how to
build a table suitable for analysis from files in heterogeneous formats.
:::

## Intuition: a ledger and a shoebox

Imagine two archives about the same houses. The first is an estate agent's
**ledger**: one line per sale, with the same columns on every line — date,
price, surface, rooms, garden yes/no. The second is a **shoebox** of photos,
handwritten notes and recorded phone calls about the same sales.

Both contain information, but only the ledger can be fed to a learning
algorithm as it is: every algorithm in this part expects a **table of numbers**
(the design matrix of @sec-ml-definitions). The shoebox must first be
turned into a ledger — photos into pixel arrays or detected features, notes
into word counts, calls into transcripts. And even a ledger needs care: is
"rooms" a quantity you can average? Is "zone" a number just because the
agency wrote it as 1, 2, 3? This chapter is about getting from files to a
trustworthy table.

## Structured and unstructured data {#sec-structured-data}

::: {#def-structured}
## Structured, semi-structured, unstructured
- **Structured** data follow a fixed **schema** known in advance: a set of
  named fields with a type each, the same for every record (a database table,
  a CSV file).
- **Semi-structured** data carry their structure *inside* the data, as tags or
  keys, and records may differ (JSON, XML, HTML).
- **Unstructured** data have no record/field organisation that a program can
  rely on: images, audio, video, free text.
:::

*In one line:* structured data come as a table; semi-structured data come as
a tree that can usually be flattened into a table; unstructured data must be
**measured** before they become a table.

| Kind | Typical formats | How it becomes a table |
|---|---|---|
| structured | CSV/TSV, spreadsheets, SQL tables | it already is one (one row per record) |
| semi-structured | JSON, XML, HTML | flatten nested fields into columns (@sec-reading-files) |
| images | PNG, JPEG | an array of pixel intensities ($h \times w \times 3$ numbers per image), or features extracted from it |
| text | plain text, documents | counts of words (bag of words), or learned numerical vectors (embeddings) |
| audio | WAV, MP3 | the amplitude sampled thousands of times per second, or its frequency content |

: Kinds of data and how they reach a learning algorithm {#tbl-data-kinds}

The relational model of Codd [@codd1970] made the structured table the
standard way to store business data, and it is still where most tabular
machine learning starts. The two snippets below show the other two routes on
toy data: a small grey-scale image *is* an array, and a set of sentences can be
turned into a table of word counts.

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# An 8x8 grey-scale "image" of a diagonal stroke: one number (0 = black ... 255 = white) per pixel
image = np.full((8, 8), 255, dtype=np.uint8)
for i in range(8):
    image[i, max(0, i - 1):i + 1] = 0
print(image.shape, image.dtype, "-> as one feature row:", image.reshape(1, -1).shape)
print(image[:3])
```

```{python}
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer

notes = ["bright flat with a large terrace",
         "dark flat, no terrace, no lift",
         "large villa with garden and terrace"]
vectorizer = CountVectorizer()                       # one column per word, one row per note
counts = vectorizer.fit_transform(notes)
pd.DataFrame(counts.toarray(), columns=vectorizer.get_feature_names_out())
```

The word-count table forgets word order ("no lift" and "lift, no" give the
same counts) — a deliberate simplification; the language models of later parts
keep the order. For the rest of this part, data are tables.

## Tidy tables {#sec-tidy}

Even a table can be organised badly for analysis. Wickham's **tidy data**
principles [@wickham2014] — the statistical counterpart of Codd's normal forms
— state what a table for analysis should look like:

1. each **variable** is a column;
2. each **observation** is a row;
3. each **type of observational unit** is a table.

A common violation is a table whose column *names* contain values. Below, the
yearly average price per zone is stored with one column per year; the
variable "year" is hidden in the header. `melt` makes the table tidy.

```{python}
wide = pd.DataFrame({"zone": ["centre", "suburbs"],
                     "2024": [4100, 2300], "2025": [4300, 2350]})
tidy = wide.melt(id_vars="zone", var_name="year", value_name="price_per_m2")
tidy["year"] = tidy["year"].astype(int)
print(wide, "\n")
print(tidy)
```

The tidy version can be filtered by year, plotted against time, and joined
with other tables by `(zone, year)`; the wide one cannot without first being
reshaped. `pivot` is the inverse operation, useful for *presenting* results.

## Types of variables {#sec-variable-types}

The first decision about every column is its **type**, because it determines
which operations make sense — and, in @sec-ch-ml-preprocessing, how it must be
encoded.

- A **quantitative** variable is a measured quantity: surface in m², price,
  temperature. It is **discrete** if it takes isolated values (number of
  rooms: 1, 2, 3, …) and **continuous** if any value in an interval is possible
  (surface).
- A **qualitative** (categorical) variable records membership of a category:
  heating type, city. It is **nominal** if the categories have no order
  (city), **ordinal** if they do (energy class A > B > C; "unfurnished <
  semi-furnished < furnished"). A **binary** variable has two categories
  (garden: yes/no).

The psychologist S. S. Stevens refined this into four **levels of
measurement** [@stevens1946], classified by which transformations of the
numbers leave their meaning unchanged:

| Level | What the numbers mean | Permissible transformations | Meaningful summaries | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **nominal** | labels | any one-to-one relabelling | counts, mode | city, postcode, customer ID |
| **ordinal** | order only | any strictly increasing map | + median, percentiles | energy class, star rating |
| **interval** | order and differences; arbitrary zero | $x \mapsto a x + b$, $a > 0$ | + mean, standard deviation | temperature in °C, calendar year |
| **ratio** | differences and ratios; true zero | $x \mapsto a x$, $a > 0$ | + ratios, geometric mean | price, surface, count of rooms |

: Stevens' levels of measurement {#tbl-stevens}

A statement about data is **meaningful** at a level if its truth does not
depend on which permissible transformation was used to record the numbers.
"House A is twice as expensive as house B" is meaningful for prices (euros or
dollars, the ratio is the same) but "Monday was twice as warm as Sunday" is
not for temperatures in °C (convert to °F and the ratio changes). The next
result explains the "meaningful summaries" column.

::: {#prp-meaningful-summaries}
## Which comparisons survive a change of scale
Let $x_1, \dots, x_n$ and $y_1, \dots, y_m$ be two groups of values and $g$ a
transformation applied to all of them.

1. If $g(t) = a t + b$ with $a > 0$, then $\bar x < \bar y \iff \overline{g(x)} < \overline{g(y)}$:
   comparisons of **means** are meaningful on interval scales.
2. If $g$ is strictly increasing, then $\operatorname{med}(g(x)) = g(\operatorname{med}(x))$
   (for odd $n$), so comparisons of **medians** are meaningful on ordinal
   scales.
3. There are strictly increasing $g$ for which $\bar x < \bar y$ but
   $\overline{g(x)} > \overline{g(y)}$: comparisons of means are **not**
   meaningful on ordinal scales.
:::

*In one line:* you may average quantities measured in units, but you may not
average labels that only express an order — the result depends on the
arbitrary numbers you chose for the labels.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-meaningful-summaries
1. $\overline{g(x)} = \frac1n\sum_i (a x_i + b) = a\bar x + b$, and the map
   $t \mapsto a t + b$ with $a > 0$ preserves order.
2. A strictly increasing $g$ preserves the sorted order of the values, so the
   middle value of $g(x_1), \dots, g(x_n)$ is $g$ of the middle value of the
   $x_i$. (For even $n$ the median is an average of two middle values and the
   identity holds only up to that average; percentiles defined as order
   statistics are preserved exactly.)
3. Counterexample: energy classes coded $1 < 2 < 3$. Group $x = (1, 1, 3)$
   has mean $5/3$; group $y = (2, 2, 2)$ has mean $2$, so $\bar x < \bar y$.
   Recode with the increasing map $g(1) = 1, g(2) = 2, g(3) = 10$: now
   $\overline{g(x)} = 4 > 2 = \overline{g(y)}$. $\blacksquare$
:::

Stevens' scheme is a guide, not a law: many statisticians treat a 1–5 rating
as roughly interval when the categories are evenly spaced in people's minds.
What it reliably flags are the gross errors: averaging postcodes or customer
IDs, or feeding a column of zone codes 1, 2, 3 to a regression as if zone 3
were "three times" zone 1. **A variable stored as a number is not
necessarily a quantity.** We return to this when we encode variables
(@sec-ch-ml-preprocessing) and in the project, whose furnishing column is a
case in point.

## Describing a variable: location, spread, shape {#sec-describing}

For a quantitative variable with values $x_1, \dots, x_n$:

- **location**: the mean $\bar x = \frac1n\sum_i x_i$ and the median;
- **spread**: the standard deviation
  $s = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_i (x_i - \bar x)^2}$ and the **interquartile
  range** (IQR, the distance between the 25th and 75th percentiles);
- **shape**: is the distribution symmetric, or does it have a long tail on one
  side?

Prices, incomes and surfaces typically have a long **right tail**: most
houses are ordinary, a few are very expensive. The mean is pulled towards the
tail and exceeds the median. The standard summary of this asymmetry is the
**skewness**, introduced into statistics by Karl Pearson [@pearson1895].

::: {#def-skewness}
## Sample skewness
With $m_k = \frac1n\sum_i (x_i - \bar x)^k$ the $k$-th central moment,
$$
g_1 = \frac{m_3}{m_2^{3/2}}, \qquad
G_1 = \frac{\sqrt{n(n-1)}}{n-2}\, g_1 .
$$ {#eq-skewness}
$G_1$ is the adjusted version reported by pandas' `Series.skew()` and by most
spreadsheets [@joanes1998]. Positive values indicate a long right tail,
negative values a long left tail, $0$ symmetry.
:::

*In one line:* skewness is the average cubed standardised deviation — cubes
keep the sign, so large deviations on one side dominate.

::: {#prp-skewness-invariance}
## Skewness does not depend on the unit of measure
For $a \neq 0$ and any $b$, the values $y_i = a x_i + b$ have
$g_1(y) = \operatorname{sign}(a)\, g_1(x)$ (and the same for $G_1$).
:::

*In one line:* changing euros into dollars or metres into feet leaves the
skewness unchanged; flipping the sign flips it.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-skewness-invariance
$\bar y = a\bar x + b$, so $y_i - \bar y = a(x_i - \bar x)$ and
$m_k(y) = a^k m_k(x)$. Then
$g_1(y) = a^3 m_3(x) / (a^2 m_2(x))^{3/2} = a^3 m_3(x)/(|a|^3 m_2(x)^{3/2})
= \operatorname{sign}(a)\,g_1(x)$. The factor relating $G_1$ to $g_1$ depends
only on $n$. $\blacksquare$
:::

::: {#exm-skewness-hand}
## Skewness by hand
Take $x = (1, 2, 3, 10)$. Mean $4$; deviations $-3, -2, -1, 6$; $m_2 =
(9+4+1+36)/4 = 12.5$; $m_3 = (-27-8-1+216)/4 = 45$. So
$g_1 = 45/12.5^{1.5} = 45/44.19 \approx 1.018$ and
$G_1 = \frac{\sqrt{12}}{2} \cdot 1.018 \approx 1.764$. The single large value
creates a strong right skew; the median ($2.5$) is well below the mean ($4$).
:::

```{python}
x = pd.Series([1, 2, 3, 10])
m = x - x.mean()
g1 = (m**3).mean() / (m**2).mean() ** 1.5
n = len(x)
G1 = np.sqrt(n * (n - 1)) / (n - 2) * g1
print(f"g1 = {g1:.3f}   G1 = {G1:.3f}   pandas skew() = {x.skew():.3f}")
print(f"after the change of unit 0.3048*x + 5: {(0.3048 * x + 5).skew():.3f};  after -x: {(-x).skew():.3f}")
```

The **logarithm** is the standard remedy for a long right tail: being
concave, it compresses large values much more than small ones
($\ln 10 - \ln 1 \approx 2.30$ but $\ln 1000 - \ln 100$ is also $2.30$), so a
tail of values spanning orders of magnitude becomes a tail of a few units. We
will see it at work on house prices below and decide in
@sec-ch-ml-regression and the project *why* it is useful — the reason is about
the errors of the model, not about making a histogram look pretty.

## Reading files into a table {#sec-reading-files}

pandas [@mckinney2010] reads every common format into a `DataFrame`
(@sec-pandas). We write a small file in each format to a temporary folder and
read it back, meeting the typical problems along the way.

```{python}
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

tmp = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())          # a private scratch folder for the examples
```

### CSV and TSV

Comma-separated values (@sec-csv, RFC 4180 [@rfc4180]) is the lingua franca
of tabular data, but "comma-separated" is a family of dialects. A file
exported by an Italian spreadsheet typically uses **semicolons** as
separators and **commas** as decimal marks, may encode text in Windows-1252
rather than UTF-8 (@sec-strings), and marks missing values in its own way.

```{python}
(tmp / "sales_it.csv").write_bytes(
    "città;prezzo;superficie;data\n"
    "Torino;245.000,50;85,5;03/02/2025\n"
    "Milano;n.d.;60;15/03/2025\n"
    "Napoli;189.900,00;102;28/04/2025\n".encode("cp1252"))

sales = pd.read_csv(tmp / "sales_it.csv", sep=";", decimal=",", thousands=".",
                    encoding="cp1252", na_values=["n.d."],
                    parse_dates=["data"], dayfirst=True)
print(sales)
print(sales.dtypes)
```

Every keyword fixed one dialect problem: without `sep=";"` pandas would see a
single column; without `decimal`/`thousands` the prices would be text;
without `encoding` the "à" of *città* would be garbled or raise an error;
without `na_values` the string `n.d.` would turn the whole price column into
text; without `parse_dates`/`dayfirst` the dates would be strings, or worse,
read month-first. **Tab-separated values** (TSV, [@ianatsv]) are the same with
`sep="\t"`; tabs rarely occur inside fields, which makes TSV more robust than
CSV.

### JSON

JSON (@sec-json, [@rfc8259]) is the usual format of web APIs. Records are
often **nested**: here each listing contains an `address` object and a list of
`features`. `pd.json_normalize` flattens nested objects into dotted column
names.

```{python}
import json

listings = [
    {"id": 101, "price": 245000, "address": {"city": "Torino", "zip": "10121"}, "features": ["lift", "balcony"]},
    {"id": 102, "price": None,   "address": {"city": "Milano", "zip": "20121"}, "features": []},
]
(tmp / "listings.json").write_text(json.dumps(listings), encoding="utf-8")

raw = json.loads((tmp / "listings.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
flat = pd.json_normalize(raw)
flat["n_features"] = flat["features"].str.len()       # a list is not a feature: summarise it
print(flat)
```

A list-valued field cannot be a column of a design matrix; it must be
summarised (its length) or expanded into indicator columns ("has lift",
"has balcony") — the one-hot encoding of @sec-ch-ml-preprocessing.

### XML

XML [@bray2008] stores the same tree structure with tags. `pd.read_xml`
turns repeated elements into rows; the `xpath` argument selects which ones.

```{python}
(tmp / "listings.xml").write_text("""<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<listings>
  <listing id="101"><city>Torino</city><price currency="EUR">245000</price><rooms>3</rooms></listing>
  <listing id="102"><city>Milano</city><price currency="EUR">310000</price><rooms>2</rooms></listing>
</listings>""", encoding="utf-8")

print(pd.read_xml(tmp / "listings.xml", xpath="//listing"))
```

Attributes (`id`) and child elements (`city`, `price`) both become columns;
the `currency` attribute of the nested `price` element is lost, a reminder to
check what a flattening keeps.

### HTML tables

Web pages publish tables in HTML (`<table>`, [@whatwghtml]).
`pd.read_html` returns a **list** of all the tables it finds, because a page
may contain several. (It needs a parser such as `lxml`.)

```{python}
from io import StringIO

page = """<html><body><h1>Average prices</h1>
<table><tr><th>Zone</th><th>€/m²</th></tr>
<tr><td>Centre</td><td>4100</td></tr><tr><td>Suburbs</td><td>2300</td></tr></table>
</body></html>"""
tables = pd.read_html(StringIO(page))
print(len(tables), "table(s) found"); print(tables[0])
```

Reading a page you do not control is fragile — the layout may change any
day — and its terms of use may forbid automated copying; prefer an official
download or API when one exists.

### Excel

Excel workbooks (`.xlsx`, the Office Open XML format [@iso29500]) contain
several **sheets**, and humans put titles, notes and merged cells above the
data. `skiprows`, `header` and `sheet_name` tell pandas where the table
starts. (Reading and writing `.xlsx` needs the `openpyxl` package.)

```{python}
with pd.ExcelWriter(tmp / "report.xlsx") as writer:
    pd.DataFrame({"note": ["Quarterly report", "Source: agency archive"]}).to_excel(
        writer, sheet_name="Q1", index=False, header=False)
    sales.drop(columns="data").to_excel(writer, sheet_name="Q1", startrow=3, index=False)

q1 = pd.read_excel(tmp / "report.xlsx", sheet_name="Q1", skiprows=3)
print(q1)
```

Excel stores numbers as numbers, so the decimal-comma problem of CSV
disappears; its own traps are dates stored as day counts, numbers stored as
text, and hidden rows or columns.

## A disciplined first look {#sec-first-look}

Before modelling, look. A short, fixed routine catches most surprises; here
it is on the house-sales data used in the project of this part — 545 sales,
whose provenance is examined in @sec-ch-project-housing.

```{python}
houses = mlbook.load_housing()
print(houses.shape)
houses.head()
```

```{python}
houses.info()
```

`info()` reports, for each column, the count of non-missing values (all 545:
no missing data here) and the **dtype**. Integer columns (`int64`) are the
quantitative ones; text columns (`str`, pandas' text type — older versions
show `object`) hold the yes/no indicators and the furnishing status. Next,
the summaries of the quantitative columns, and the categories of the others.

```{python}
houses.describe().T.style.format(precision=1, thousands=",")
```

```{python}
for col in houses.select_dtypes(exclude="number").columns:
    print(f"{col:17s}", houses[col].value_counts().to_dict())
```

Now classify the columns (@tbl-stevens). `price` and `area` are ratio-scale
continuous quantities; `bedrooms`, `bathrooms`, `stories` and `parking` are
discrete counts (ratio scale); six columns are **binary**; and
`furnishingstatus` has three categories with a natural order
(unfurnished < semi-furnished < furnished) — **ordinal**. Finally, the shape
of the target:

```{python}
#| label: fig-price-skew
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of the 545 sale prices (left) and of their natural logarithm (right). The price has a long right tail; its logarithm is nearly symmetric."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.2))
ax1.hist(houses["price"] / 1e6, bins=30, color=mlbook.COLORS[0], edgecolor="#fcfcfb")
ax1.set_xlabel("price (millions of the data set's units)"); ax1.set_ylabel("number of sales")
ax1.set_title(f"price: skewness {houses['price'].skew():.2f}")
ax2.hist(np.log(houses["price"]), bins=30, color=mlbook.COLORS[2], edgecolor="#fcfcfb")
ax2.set_xlabel("ln(price)")
ax2.set_title(f"ln(price): skewness {np.log(houses['price']).skew():.2f}")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
print(f"mean {houses['price'].mean():,.0f}  >  median {houses['price'].median():,.0f}")
```

The price is right-skewed (the mean exceeds the median by about 10%), and its
logarithm is almost symmetric. This first look already gives three decisions
for later chapters: the yes/no columns need encoding, the furnishing column
needs an encoding that respects its type, and the target may be better
modelled on a logarithmic scale.

::: {.project-link}
**In the project.** The project's data come as a single CSV file, so the
reading step is one line; the work is in the **first look**. Classifying the
columns (@tbl-stevens) shows that `furnishingstatus` is ordinal, not a
quantity; @fig-price-skew shows the right skew of the price. The copy of the
file distributed with the course stores furnishing as the integers 0, 1, 2 —
and, as we will find in @sec-ch-project-housing, the codes are not even in the
natural order. A number is not always a quantity.
:::

## Common pitfalls

::: {.callout-warning}
## Watch out
- **Trusting the default CSV dialect.** Check separator, decimal mark,
  thousands separator, encoding and missing-value markers on the first rows of
  the raw file before reading it.
- **Treating codes as quantities**: postcodes, IDs, zone numbers, ordinal
  codes. Averaging or regressing on them is meaningless
  (@prp-meaningful-summaries).
- **A numeric column read as text** because of one stray value (`n.d.`,
  `-`, `1.234,5`): every later computation silently fails or errors.
- **Dates read as strings**, or day and month swapped (`03/02` is 3 February
  in Italy, 2 March in the USA).
- **Losing information when flattening** JSON/XML (attributes, lists).
- **Scraping web pages** that change layout or forbid it; prefer official
  downloads or APIs.
- **Skipping the first look.** Shape, dtypes, missing counts, summaries,
  category counts and one histogram take two minutes and save hours.
:::

## Summary

- **Structured** data have a fixed schema; **semi-structured** data (JSON,
  XML, HTML) carry it in tags; **unstructured** data (images, text, audio) must
  be turned into numbers — pixels, word counts, embeddings.
- A **tidy** table has one variable per column and one observation per row;
  `melt` and `pivot` reshape between wide and long forms.
- Variable **types** — nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio; discrete or
  continuous — decide which summaries are meaningful: means need at least an
  interval scale, medians an ordinal one.
- **Skewness** $g_1 = m_3/m_2^{3/2}$ (pandas reports the adjusted $G_1$) is
  unit-free; a long right tail is often tamed by a logarithm.
- pandas reads CSV/TSV (`sep`, `decimal`, `thousands`, `encoding`,
  `na_values`, `parse_dates`), JSON (`json_normalize`), XML (`read_xml`), HTML
  (`read_html`) and Excel (`read_excel`, `sheet_name`, `skiprows`).
- A **first look** — shape, `info`, `describe`, category counts, a histogram
  of the target — precedes any model.

## Exercises

::: {#exr-ml2-types}
Classify each variable by Stevens' level and say whether it is discrete or
continuous: (a) the floor number of a flat (ground floor = 0); (b) the energy
class A4…G; (c) the year of construction; (d) the condominium fee in €/month;
(e) the ISTAT code of the municipality; (f) the number of bathrooms.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
(a) interval, discrete: differences are meaningful (three floors up), but
the zero is a convention (basements are $-1$), so "twice as high" is not;
(b) ordinal, discrete;
(c) interval (year 0 is arbitrary; "built twice as late" is meaningless),
discrete; (d) ratio, continuous; (e) **nominal** despite being a number,
discrete; (f) ratio, discrete.
:::

::: {#exr-ml2-skew}
Compute $g_1$ and $G_1$ by hand for $x = (2, 4, 4, 4, 6)$ and for
$x = (1, 1, 1, 1, 6)$, then check with pandas. Which is skewed, and in which
direction?
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
The first sample is symmetric around 4: $m_3 = 0$, so $g_1 = G_1 = 0$. The
second has mean 2, deviations $(-1,-1,-1,-1,4)$, $m_2 = 20/5 = 4$,
$m_3 = (-4 + 64)/5 = 12$, $g_1 = 12/8 = 1.5$,
$G_1 = \frac{\sqrt{20}}{3}\cdot 1.5 \approx 2.236$: right-skewed.
```{python}
print(pd.Series([2, 4, 4, 4, 6]).skew(), pd.Series([1, 1, 1, 1, 6]).skew())
```
:::

::: {#exr-ml2-median-ordinal}
A hotel chain codes reviews as poor = 1, fair = 2, good = 3, excellent = 4.
Hotel A has reviews (1, 4, 4) and hotel B (3, 3, 3). Which has the higher
mean? Find an order-preserving recoding that reverses the comparison. Does the
comparison of medians change?
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
Means: A $= (1+4+4)/3 = 3$ and B $= 3$ — tied. Recode excellent $= 3.5$
(still above good $= 3$): A $= (1 + 7)/3 \approx 2.67 <$ B $= 3$. Recode
excellent $= 10$ instead: A $= (1 + 20)/3 = 7 >$ B $= 3$. Two legitimate,
order-preserving codings give opposite answers, so the comparison of means is
not meaningful. The medians are A $=$ excellent and B $=$ good under every
order-preserving coding, as @prp-meaningful-summaries guarantees.
:::

::: {#exr-ml2-read}
Write a TSV file in which the second column contains numbers with a
thousands separator (`1,250`) and one row uses `?` for a missing value. Read
it so that the column is numeric. Then save the same data as JSON with
`DataFrame.to_json(orient="records")` and read it back. Is anything lost?
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
(tmp / "t.tsv").write_text("item\tamount\nA\t1,250\nB\t?\nC\t980\n", encoding="utf-8")
t = pd.read_csv(tmp / "t.tsv", sep="\t", thousands=",", na_values=["?"])
print(t.dtypes.to_dict())
t.to_json(tmp / "t.json", orient="records")
print(pd.read_json(tmp / "t.json"))
```
The amount becomes `float64` (a missing value forces floats, because `NaN` is
a float); JSON stores the missing value as `null` and it comes back as `NaN`.
Nothing is lost here, but JSON does not store dtypes: integers that were
floats only because of a `NaN` stay floats, and dates come back as numbers or
strings unless you say otherwise.
:::

## Further reading {.unnumbered}

- @wickham2014 — tidy data, with many reshaping examples (in R, but the ideas
  map one-to-one onto `melt`/`pivot`).
- @stevens1946 — four pages that still frame how we think about variable
  types.
- @mckinney2022, ch. 6 — reading and writing data with pandas, by its author.
- @codd1970 — the relational model, the ancestor of every structured table.
- @joanes1998 — the three sample skewness estimators and their bias.
- @rfc4180, @rfc8259, @bray2008 — the specifications of CSV, JSON and XML.
